title: Attacking a reputation
core: All five are ways of talking someone down — lowering how they are regarded, by the listener or by the world. They differ on three axes: whether the attack must be **false**, whether it must be **public**, and how **wicked** the target ends up looking. At the low end the victim merely seems small and unimpressive; at the high end they seem evil, and the attacker seems like a liar. Most of these words judge the speaker as much as the target.

words.nuance: The only one that needs no audience and makes no accusation — **belittle** shrinks, it does not blacken. The target ends up looking minor, not wicked, and the classic scene is one-on-one and perfectly polite: a boss, a parent, a rival. It also uniquely attaches to non-persons — a fear, a grievance, an achievement can be belittled.

Where *belittle* can be one condescending remark, **denigrate** is the sustained running-down of someone's worth or reputation, and the word itself rules the attack undeserved. Crucially it requires no lie — unfair emphasis, sneering, faint praise all denigrate. Formal: the verb of editorials and HR complaints.

Falsity and publicity are both mandatory here — **defame** is the legal-technical member, splitting into libel and slander. Truth is a complete defence: however savage the statement, if it is accurate you have not defamed. Note the shift in victim — *belittle* damages how you see yourself, **defame** rewrites how everyone else sees you.

The only one that specifies the *content* of the attack: **vilify** paints the target as evil, contemptible, someone fit to be hated. It needs a crowd and time — a press campaign, not a courtroom claim — and unlike *defame* it needs no provable lie, only distortion. It usually arrives as "unfairly vilified," the writer taking the target's side.

The only noun: **calumny** names the lie itself, or the practice of telling it, so it takes articles and plurals — *a calumny*, *spread calumnies*. It out-moralises *defame*: same falsehood, but with deliberate malice and the speaker's disgust attached, and none of the legal machinery. Use it when you want the accusation to sound shameful rather than actionable.

exam_note: The trap is the falsity axis: only **defame** and **calumny** entail a lie, so a sentence stipulating "though every word was true" kills them and rewards **denigrate**/**vilify** — and **calumny**'s noun slot is often the cleanest structural giveaway.
